# Chapter exercise: Joins: Attribute and Spatial {.unnumbered}

**Matching Tables by Name and by Place**

This exercise goes with **Chapter 15, Joins: Attribute and Spatial**. It builds on the tidyverse, tmap, and coordinate systems exercises. It should take you about **one hour**. Read this whole section before you start.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}

## Purpose

**Skills you'll practice.** By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

1. Combine two tables with `inner_join()`, `left_join()`, `right_join()`, and `full_join()`, and predict how many rows each returns.
2. Name the key with `join_by()`, including when the key columns have different names.
3. Find the rows that didn't match with `anti_join()`, and fix a key that doesn't match.
4. Describe the cardinality of a relationship.
5. Join by location with `st_join()`, and count the points in each polygon with a summarized join.
6. Find the nearest feature with a distance join, after projecting both layers.

**Knowledge you'll gain.** You'll attach Census populations to North Carolina cities, map how median income changed across the states, find the London boroughs with the most bike-share stations, and find the nearest airport to ten North Carolina cities.

**Why this matters.** Data almost never arrives in one table. Census counts come without boundaries, boundaries come without the counts, and points such as schools or crimes need to be matched to the neighborhood they fall in. Joining is how you'll bring your final project's data together. A join that silently drops or duplicates rows is one of the most common hidden errors in data analysis, so checking the row count before and after every join is a habit worth building now.

## Task

Work through Parts 1 to 7 in order, top to bottom. In each part:

- Read the short explanation, then do each step marked with a bullet (•).
- Wherever you see `___`, replace it with the missing code **before** you run the chunk. A chunk with `___` in it won't run.
- **Before you run** each join, predict how many rows it will return. Then run it and check.
- Answer each question (**Q1**, **Q2**, ...) in a sentence or two of Markdown, where it says *Your answer here.*

| Part | What you'll do | About |
|:-----|:---------------|:------|
| 1 | Set up your file and load the data | 3 min |
| 2 | Four kinds of join on two small tables | 12 min |
| 3 | Join income data to state boundaries | 10 min |
| 4 | When names don't match | 7 min |
| 5 | Spatial joins: which borough is each station in? | 13 min |
| 6 | Distance joins: the nearest airport | 10 min |
| 7 | Reflect, knit, and turn in | 5 min |

**Turn in** your `.Rmd` file and your knitted `.html` file on Canvas.

## Criteria for success

Use this checklist before you turn your work in. Each item matches a row of the rubric below.

- [ ] The file knits to HTML with no errors, and every map appears in it.
- [ ] Every `___` has been filled in, and every chunk runs.
- [ ] Every question (Q1 to Q11) has an answer in complete sentences, with row counts and names from your output.
- [ ] Before each join, you predicted the number of rows (in your head or in a comment), and checked it after.
- [ ] Both layers in every spatial join are in the same projected CRS.
- [ ] Every map has a title, a legend title, and credits with your name and the data source.
- [ ] No `install.packages()` line is anywhere in the file.
- [ ] The three reflection questions are answered.

| Criterion | Full credit | Partial credit | No credit |
|:----------|:------------|:---------------|:----------|
| Knits (2 pts) | Knits to HTML with every map showing | Knits, but some chunks have errors | Doesn't knit, or no HTML turned in |
| Join code (5 pts) | Every blank filled in correctly; right join type and key each time | Most correct | Many blanks missing or wrong |
| Questions (9 pts) | Q1 to Q11 answered with row counts, names, and reasons | Some answers missing, wrong, or without reasons | Most answers missing |
| Maps (2 pts) | Both maps finished with title, legend title, and credits | Labels missing | Maps missing |
| Style (1 pt) | Pipe for chains, `join_by()` for keys, no `install.packages()` | | Several problems |
| Reflection (1 pt) | All three answered | | Missing |

**What a good answer looks like.** Here is a question, a weak answer, and a strong one.

> *Question:* Why did the join return fewer rows than the first table?
>
> *Weak answer:* "Some rows were dropped."
>
> *Strong answer:* "`inner_join()` keeps only rows with a match in both tables. `us_states` has the lower 48 states and DC, so Alaska and Hawaii in `us_states_df` had no match and were dropped: 51 rows became 49. `anti_join()` lists them."

The strong answer names the join type, says which rows were lost and why, gives the counts, and shows how to check.

**IMPORTANT!** Save often. Before you knit, choose **Run > Restart R and Run All Chunks** to make sure every chunk works from a fresh start.
